items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: The right place at the right time and three months later I was in the Count Basie Orchestra, July 27, 1953.

ctx.x: The right place at the right time and three months later I was in the Count Basie Orchestra, July 27, 1953.
Had you had a chance while you were in the service to still be listening to recordings of them?

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: On the 27th of July 1953, I flew to New York to join Count Basie.

ctx.x: That’s a hell of a grapevine.

Yeah, one hell of a grapevine. I said, “No one knows I’m in town.” He said, “Count Basie’s playing over at the Graystone Ballroom tonight, so why don’t you go over there and check it out?” Surely enough I went over there, still dressed in my army uniform. I found out that Count Basie was looking for a replacement for “Lockjaw” Davis. Ernie and Jimmy Wilkins were both in the band. They recognized me. They said, “Oh, hey, man, we recommended you for the band.” So Basie auditioned me. I played two songs, Body and…

The 25th of September 1998. I’m William Brower, talking with Frank Foster. Recording is Matt Watson. This is for the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Program. Can you describe your coming to meet Basie, what the actual moment -- do you recollect that moment when you’re summoned and you come and you meet him? What happened? Describe that moment.

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: if something didn’t sound good in rehearsal, Basie nixed it. It just wouldn’t get played.

ctx.x: Okay, the chart was inspired by my first wife putting on stockings. This was in 1954 BPH (before panty hose), when stockings were really stockings. You know and all the appendages, yes garter belts, I didn’t want to say it. But and she used to put them on and the light would hit her legs in a certain way. And it just, the phrase “Shiny Stockings” just came to me, looking at this repeatedly, repeatedly, you know. Something happens long enough to you and you get an idea about it. And so I put it into a song. But…

something there, he must have realized that, well the guys are all evil and tired, and they’re not putting their hundred percent, but there’s something in there. He must have. Because that’s one of the few charts that I ever contributed that Basie years later came to me and said, “hey, Foss, that ‘Shiny Stockings,’” he said, “you really put one down that time.”
